implementation_notes: Go expresses the pattern with its own primitives rather than a framework: the recipient set is a slice computed per message (channels, client handles or queue names), a for-range loop starts one goroutine per recipient for the copy-and-send step, and sync.WaitGroup supplies the completion barrier - the fan-out/fan-in shape documented in the Go blog's pipelines article. Nothing has to be built beyond ownership rules: errgroup.Group adds error propagation and context cancellation when a failed recipient should abort the fan-out, and buffered channels absorb short bursts. A hand-written router component only earns its place when policy (retries, dead-lettering, allow-lists) must be shared by many call sites.
pitfalls: A blocked or unbuffered recipient channel parks its goroutine forever; without a context-plus-select timeout the fan-out never returns and every goroutine leaks.
Closing a channel while a sender still writes to it panics, and goroutines are not garbage collected - ownership of each recipient channel must be unambiguous.
Capturing the range variable directly made every goroutine send to the last recipient before Go 1.22; the hazard returns when the toolchain or the module's go directive is older.
